title: Polish both faces of a blank on a running buffing wheel without letting it snatch
instruction: Polish both faces of the aluminium blank on the buffing wheel, then stand it back in its rack.
context: Polishers present work to a buffing wheel below its centreline, on the face running down toward the work rest, with the part's edge on the rest: the wheel's drag then pushes the part onto the rest. Held higher, or where the rest cannot take the drag, the same drag snatches the part out of the hand and throws it, a common buffing injury. Here the drag is contact friction: on the rest below the centreline the blank stays put, above it the blank is twisted out of the grip. A whole face must be worked across the 25 mm wheel, and the end under the fingers needs a change of grip. Bench buffers are everyday tools in home, school and hobby workshops (jewellery, knives, car trim), not only in polishing trades. Unlike #452 (wait for a grinder to stop), the wheel runs throughout. Unlike #671 (set tool-rest gaps) and #871 (mount a wheel), nothing is adjusted. Unlike #674 (hold a smoother still on a turntable), the part is braced on a support and moved across the wheel.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left). Bench buffer: a fixed grey cast-iron double-ended buffer, motor 12 x 16 x 13 cm on a 16 x 20 cm base, centred at x 36, y 0, its spindle along y 10 cm above the bench. Wheels: two 15 cm, 2.5 cm wide spiral-sewn cotton buffs dressed with tan polishing compound (300 g each) at y -20 and y +20, running at 2 rev/s with their front faces moving down toward the arms. Work rests: a fixed steel plate 6 x 6 x 0.6 cm on a steel post under the front of each wheel, top 3.7 cm above the bench, back edge 3 mm from the wheel. Blank: a 6061 aluminium flat bar 10 x 4 x 1 cm (108 g), standing on its long edge, faces toward and away from the buffer, in a fixed steel rack (two 11 x 1 x 1 cm bars 2 mm clear of each face) centred at x 19, y -20; the face away from the buffer (face B) has a small dark scribed mark near one end. On a real rig the buffer runs only inside the robot's interlocked, guarded cell, with a hood over each wheel except its lower front working quadrant and a fixed polycarbonate catch screen and tray below the rests; nobody enters while it runs (README: 'Real-world rig: guarding and protection').
scoring: From PhysX contact reports between the blank and the wheels, read after every physics step, and the recorded poses (on a real rig: a wrist force sensor and the trial video, or a gloss reading per strip after the trial). A physics step polishes a face only when a wheel touches it (contact points at 0.5 mm separation or less, on the face, not its edges, on the wheel's down-running front below the spindle) and presses it (at least 1 N of contact force along the face's normal); a face hovering near the rim earns nothing. Each face is divided into ten 10 mm strips along its length: the strips under the wheel's 25 mm width get the step's time, a strip is polished after 0.5 s, and a face is polished with 8 of its 10 strips (held still in one place, a face covers at most 3). Latched 0 for the rest of the trial: the blank turns more than 25 deg in the gripper holding it while a corner is within 2 cm of a wheel's rim (snatched), or it moves faster than 0.5 m/s (flung). Otherwise 0.25 per polished face; 1.0 with both faces polished and the blank back in its rack (centre within 6 mm across and 2 cm along the slot, upright within 10 deg, on the bench, either face forward), let go (both grippers 2.5 cm clear) and still, success when held 1 s. Scored at the last step. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: Stand the blank back in its rack, face B away from the buffer; the wheels keep running (on a real rig: stop the buffer and wait for the guard lock to release before entering the cell, then restart it from outside); the buffer, rests and rack do not move.
fidelity: Rigid boxes, one friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), blank-wheel too. Each wheel is a 36-sided rigid buff on a PhysX revolute joint with a velocity drive (2 rev/s, 0.5 N*m*s/rad), not 1,750 rpm; Coulomb drag does not depend on speed. No cloth give, compound or heat: polish is pressed contact (PhysX contact reports, 1 N or more) credited over the wheel's 25 mm width, as a cloth buff bears; the rigid one may touch an edge. The snatch is the blank slipping round in the finger pads (tried in sim).
